definition.text: Maximum sustainable yield (MSY) is, in theory, the largest catch that can be taken from a stock year after year for an indefinite period.

facts.text: MSY keeps a population at the size where it grows fastest, harvesting the individuals that would otherwise be added to it.
Small populations grow slowly because few fish breed; near carrying capacity crowding stops growth; in between, at half carrying capacity in the logistic model, the surplus is largest.
Modern fisheries models refine this, putting MSY at around 30% of the unexploited population size.
MSY is usually higher than the optimum sustainable yield and the maximum economic yield.
It became popular in the 1950s and was adopted as the main goal by bodies such as the IWC and ICCAT.
A 1955 international MSY treaty let foreign fleets fish off any coast unless the coastal nation proved its fish were overfished.
MSY was written into the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea even as scientists questioned it.

definition.text: The simplest harvest model subtracts a constant catch H from logistic population growth and finds where catch equals growth.

facts.text: The population is at equilibrium when it stops growing, that is when dN/dt = 0 and growth equals harvest.
With logistic growth the maximum harvest equals one-fourth of carrying capacity K times the intrinsic growth rate r, reached at half of K.
Below MSY there are two equilibria: the higher is stable, the lower collapses toward extinction after any shock.
The MSY point itself is semi-stable, a knife-edge where a small fall in numbers spirals to extinction unless catch is cut.
Harvesting a fixed percentage or a constant effort instead of a fixed number avoids some of these instabilities.
Any harvest pulls a population below its original carrying capacity; sustainable harvest is possible only because of density dependence.

title: Criticism of maximum sustainable yield

definition.text: Maximum sustainable yield, though widely used by agencies managing fish, forests and wildlife, has been heavily criticised by ecologists on theoretical and practical grounds.

facts.text: In 1977 Peter Larkin argued it risked populations, ignored spatial variation and other species, counted benefits but not costs, and bent to political pressure.
Estimates suffer from poor model assumptions, unreliable data and treating all fish as identical regardless of age or size.
A fixed yearly MSY catch ignores natural swings in abundance and usually depletes stocks, so scientists now speak of maximum average yield.
Early New Zealand orange roughy quotas assumed fast breeding, but the fish turned out long-lived and slow, and stocks were depleted.
Many conservation biologists regard MSY as dangerous and misused, and it is blamed for collapses of many fisheries.

contested_note: Agencies still use MSY widely while many ecologists and conservation biologists consider it dangerous.

definition.text: Fisheries science is the academic discipline of understanding and managing fisheries.

facts.text: It draws on oceanography, marine and freshwater biology, ecology, population dynamics, economics, statistics and decision analysis.
New fields have grown out of it, such as bioeconomics and fisheries law.
Research uses specialised vessels that tow nets, sample plankton and water, and carry acoustic fish-finders.
Fedor Baranov's 1918 catch equation is perhaps the most used equation in fisheries modelling.
Michael Graham's 'Great Law of Fishing' holds that unlimited fisheries become unprofitable.

definition.text: The Gordon-Schaefer model is a bioeconomic model of a fishery that combines fish population growth with the costs and revenues of fishing.

facts.text: It accounts for biological growth rates, carrying capacity, and total and marginal costs and revenues, and can compute maximum sustainable yield.
It compares three scenarios: a monopoly owner, the biological optimum of MSY, and open access.
A profit-maximising owner fishes until marginal revenue equals marginal cost; monopolies produce less at higher prices than competitive markets.
Under open access, each year's catch is set by demand and costs, ignoring effects on future years.
Gordon's 1954 analysis showed that under open access entry continues until total value minus costs is zero.
